messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajan is a 58-year-old South Asian man, married and working as a Product Manager at a mid-sized technology firm in the Pacific Northwest. He was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure to his primary care physician of persistent sleep disturbance and what he described, quietly and with evident shame, as an inability to "function normally" since an experience of detention and torture he endured approximately four years ago while visiting family in his country of origin. He had been held for several days by state security forces, subjected to prolonged physical abuse, hooding, and repeated interrogations conducted in a language he could not fully follow — a disorienting blur of shouted commands, overlapping voices, and incomprehensible exchanges that left him unable to distinguish threat from procedure. The sound of sirens had accompanied his transfer between facilities. By the time he was released and eventually returned to the United States, the damage had already taken root.

In the months that followed, Rajan began to carry a belief that has since become foundational to his suffering: that something intrinsic to who he is had made him a target, that he had been identified and selected because of some flaw or quality he could not name but could not dismiss. Alongside this was a corrosive mistrust — of colleagues, of strangers, of systems he had once navigated without anxiety. He had come to believe that people, broadly, could not be trusted, and that nothing genuinely good lay ahead of him. These appraisals did not remain abstract. They drove him steadily toward a life organized around containment and avoidance: he began refusing assignments that required travel, declined team meetings he judged as unpredictable, and quietly restructured his days at work to minimize any situation he anticipated as stressful. He also found himself unable to pass a uniformed security guard in the office lobby without rerouting — a small but daily act of avoidance that his colleagues noticed without understanding.

The same convictions that shaped his avoidance also kept his nervous system in a state of unrelenting vigilance. Rajan could not relax even in environments he consciously recognized as safe. At night, he woke repeatedly to check whether the bedroom door was locked, whether his wife was still beside him, whether the sounds from the street were ordinary. He startled violently at unexpected touch — a hand on his shoulder from a well-meaning colleague during a product review had once caused him to knock over his chair. This chronic state of alert, never fully discharged, meant that the threshold for perceived danger remained perpetually low, and the world was full of things that crossed it. The sirens of emergency vehicles, audible from the open-plan office where he worked, sent a jolt through him that he could neither suppress nor explain to those nearby. Patches of incomprehensible chatter — a foreign-language phone call overheard in the corridor, a multilingual meeting where voices overlapped — pulled him back with a force that felt physical. And sometimes, without clear external cause, a wave of dizziness would rise through him, and his body would seem to be telling him something his mind had not yet registered.

Rajan's attempts to manage these experiences had, over time, made them worse. His constant scanning of his body for signs of injury or danger — a habit formed in detention, where physical damage had to be privately assessed — now amplified every somatic sensation into potential evidence of threat, which in turn made the dizziness and the startle responses feel more alarming and more confirming of his belief that he was fundamentally unsafe. His avoidance of stressors narrowed his world steadily, and the narrowing itself became proof, to him, that he was broken in some irreversible way — which deepened his conviction that nothing good could come. The loop had been running for years before he named it as a problem.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a conversation with his wife, who told him, carefully and with evident grief, that she no longer recognized the man she had married. He had heard her. What he most fears, sitting across from a clinician for the first time, is that she is right. What he most hopes — though he holds the hope at arm's length — is that she is wrong.
